    History. What is the history of The Gambia?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    The Gambia, West Africa's smallest nation, has a history defined by its river. Formerly part of the Ghana, Mali, and Songhai empires, the region became a British colonial entity in the 19th century after Portuguese trade, focusing on the Gambia River. It gained independence in 1965, becoming a republic in 1970 and experiencing a democratic transition in 2017. 
    Key Historical Periods:
    • Early History:
      The area was historically part of the Ghana and Mali empires, serving as a trade route for gold and slaves via Arab traders. 
    • European Contact:
      The Portuguese reached the coast in the 15th century, followed by British establishment in 1661. 
    • Colonial Period:
      The Gambia was administered as part of British West Africa (1821–1843, 1866–1889) before becoming a separate colony. The economy became heavily dependent on peanut exports. 
    • Independence (1965):
      The Gambia gained independence on February 18, 1965, with Dawda Jawara as prime minister. 
    • Republic and Recent History:
      It became a republic on April 24, 1970. Following a 1994 coup, Yahya Jammeh ruled for over two decades before losing the 2016 election to Adama Barrow, marking a democratic turning point in 2017. 
    • Senegambia Confederation:
      A brief confederation (1982-1989) with Senegal followed a coup attempt in 1981. 
    The Gambia is now known as a parliamentary democracy with a diverse population, including Mandinka, Fula, Wolof, Jola, and Serahuli groups.

      Tourist Destinations. What are the popular tourist destinations in The Gambia?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      The Gambia offers a blend of Atlantic beaches, wildlife, and history, with top destinations including the lively Kololi and Kotu beaches, the monkey-filled Bijilo Forest Park, and the historical Kunta Kinteh Island. Visitors frequently explore the Kachikally Crocodile Pool, the River Gambia National Park, and the vibrant Albert Market in Banjul. 
      Top Beach Destinations
      • Kololi Beach: Known for its lively atmosphere, bustling Senegambia strip, and nearby hotels. 
      • Kotu Beach: A popular, slightly quieter choice with stunning scenery. 
      • Sanyang Beach (Paradise Beach): Famous for its natural beauty, golden sand, and weekend beach bars. 
      • Bijilo Beach: Located near Bijilo Forest Park, offering a more relaxed environment. 
      Nature and Wildlife
      • Bijilo Forest Park: A coastal park popular for trekking and spotting green vervet monkeys. 
      • River Gambia National Park: Famous for its chimpanzee rehabilitation project on Baboon Island. 
      • Abuko Nature Reserve: The country's first nature reserve, offering trails to see birds and crocodiles. 
      • Makasutu Culture Forest: An eco-tourism site with mangroves and jungle areas. 
      Cultural and Historical Sites
      • Kunta Kinteh Island (formerly James Island): A UNESCO World Heritage site associated with the slave trade. 
      • Kachikally Crocodile Pool: A sacred, historic site in Bakau where visitors can get close to crocodiles. 
      • Banjul: The capital city, featuring the iconic Arch 22, the National Museum, and the Albert Market. 
      • Wassu Stone Circles: Ancient megaliths that are a UNESCO World Heritage site. 
      Experiences 
      • Tanji Fishing Village: Excellent for viewing the bustling, colorful local fishing industry and, optionally, visiting the nearby museum.
      • Camel Riding: Available on some beaches, such as Sanyang.

        AI Overview
        The Gambia has a young, rapidly growing population of approximately 2.76–2.88 million people (2026 est.), with a median age under 20 years. The population is predominantly Muslim (over 92–96%), with major ethnic groups including the Mandinka, Fula, Wolof, Jola, and Serahuli. The nation is experiencing high urbanization, with over 60% of people living in urban or town areas. 
        Key Demographic Data
        • Population: ~2.88 million (2026 est.). 
        • Median Age: ~18.8–19.4 years, indicating a very young population. 
        • Population Growth: High, with an annual growth rate around 2.2%. 
        • Age Structure: ~40-42% of the population is under 15 years old. 
        • Urbanization: ~62.2% urban (2026 est.), reflecting rapid migration to cities. 
        Ethnic Groups and Religion
        • Ethnic Groups: Mandinka (42%), Fula (18%), Wolof (16%), Jola (10%), Serahuli (9%), and others. 
        • Religion: Muslim (92.2%–96.4%), with small Christian and animist minorities. 
        • Languages: English is official, alongside indigenous languages: Mandinka, Wolof, Fula, and Jola. 
        Health and Household
        • Life Expectancy: Approximately 64–66 years. 
        • Fertility Rate: ~3.7–3.98 children per woman, which is among the highest in the world. 
        • Household Size: Large, with an average household size estimated between 6.9 and 8.3 persons. 
        Location 
        • The Gambia is a small West African nation almost entirely surrounded by Senegal.

          AI Overview
          +7
          The Gambia, Africa's smallest non-island country, is a narrow nation surrounding the Gambia River, almost entirely enclosed by Senegal
          . Known as the "Smiling Coast," it has a population of over 2.4 million, a popular tropical coastline, and a culture rich in drumming, dancing, and history. The capital is Banjul, and English is the official language. 
          Key Aspects of The Gambia: 
          • Geography: A narrow strip of land, approx.
            , following the lower Gambia River, primarily consisting of savannah and mangrove swamps.
          • Culture: The culture is rooted in various ethnic groups—primarily Malinke, Wolof, Fulani, Diola, and Soninke—and is known for its hospitality.
          • Economy:
            The economy is heavily dependent on agriculture, especially peanuts, and a thriving tourism industry geared towards beaches, nature, and birdwatching.
          • History: A former British colony, it gained independence in 1965.
          • Religion: The population is predominantly Muslim, with a small Christian minority, and is known for its peaceful religious coexistence.
          • Major Cities: The capital is Banjul; however, Serekunda and Brikama are the largest urban centers. 
          Important Information for Visitors: 
          • Language: Official language is English, though local languages like Wolof and Mandinka are widely spoken.
          • Currency: The Dalasi (
            GMDcap G cap M cap D
            ).
          • Best Time to Visit: The dry season, roughly November to May, offers the best weather for beaches and wildlife.
          • Attractions: Kunta Kinteh Island (historical site), Bijilo Forest Park, Kachikally Crocodile Pool, and diverse beach resorts.

          About

          Description

          The Gambia is a small West African country, bounded by Senegal, with a narrow Atlantic coastline. It's known for its diverse ecosystems around the central Gambia River. Abundant wildlife in its Kiang West National Park and Bao Bolong Wetland Reserve includes monkeys, leopards, hippos, hyenas and rare birds. The capital, Banjul, and nearby Serrekunda offer access to beaches. ― Google
          Capital: Banjul
          Currency: Gambian Dalasi
          Official language: English
          President: Adama Barrow
          Population: 2.76 million (2024) World Bank
          Dialing code: +220
